opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that it was simply too early. The idea was right, but the foundation wasn't there.

Back in 2016, that project, World of Bits, and more broadly Universe, tried to have an agent operate a computer the way a human does. It looked at pixels on the screen and output keyboard and mouse actions. The plan was to train it mostly with reinforcement learning, plus some behavior cloning from human demonstrations. That was the mainstream thinking at the time, because deep RL had just had huge wins in Atari and Go. People thought, if RL can play Atari from pixels, why not the web?

But the web is a completely different thing from Atari. To book a flight or fill in a form, you first need to understand language. You need to read the instructions, understand what's on the page, and have some common sense about how websites work. In 2016 we had no pretrained language models. There was no GPT, no BERT. So the agent started from zero. It had to learn what a "button" is, what "submit" means, and what the task is even asking, all from a very sparse reward signal. The exploration problem was hopeless. If you click randomly on a webpage, the chance you accidentally complete a meaningful multi-step task is essentially zero. So you get no reward and no learning.

In the end, people could only get it to work on very simple mini tasks, like clicking a specific button or typing something into a box. It never generalized to the real, open web.

Looking back, the lesson is very clear. RL is not something you apply from scratch to the real world. RL needs a strong prior. Today's agents work because we first pretrain a large model on internet-scale data. That model already understands language, roughly knows how computers and websites work, and can reason a bit. Then RL is used to sharpen that ability, align it with goals, and make it robust over long horizons. The pretrained model solves the exploration problem for you. It gives you reasonable actions to begin with, so the reward is no longer impossibly sparse.

So I wouldn't say the people were wrong. The vision of a general-purpose agent was exactly right. It's basically what everyone is building now. But the order was reversed. You need the knowledge first, and then RL. In 2016 they tried to let RL do everything, and that's why it didn't work.

r001.rationale: It says there were no pretrained language models in 2016 and the agent had to start from zero, identifying the missing model foundation as a reason for failure.

r002.rationale: It does not identify a lack of people collecting data for labeling as a reason for failure.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say I was only on the edge of that — I joined OpenAI in 2017, so I saw the aftermath more than the project itself. But the effort, World of Bits, was actually a very natural idea for the time. The logic was simple: the Atari results had just come out, you could train an agent to play games from pixels, so why not treat the browser as one giant game? Pixels in, mouse and keyboard out, and the whole internet becomes your environment.

In hindsight, I think it failed for three reasons, and the ordering matters.

The first is the reward problem. In Atari the score is given to you. On the web, what does "success" even mean for a task like "book me a flight to Boston"? Somebody has to write that reward function, and either you hand-craft it for every task, which doesn't scale, or you fake it with proxies that the agent immediately games. So the environment was general, but the supervision wasn't. You ended up with a few hundred tiny hand-built tasks — click this button, fill this form — and the agent would learn each one from scratch.

The second is that reinforcement learning from pixels is incredibly sample-inefficient, and the web is non-stationary. A game is a fixed program; a website changes its layout next week. Every time the environment drifts, your policy is garbage. Even if you solved one site, nothing transferred to the next one, because the agent had no notion of what a "submit button" is in general. It had only memorized where the pixels were.

And the third reason, which I think is the real one, is that the agent had no prior. It didn't know language, it didn't know what a form is, it didn't know what a human would want. It was starting from zero and trying to acquire common sense through trial and error, and the amount of experience you'd need for that is essentially infinite. People at the time understood this intuitively but didn't have the alternative.

So the project wasn't wrong about the destination. It was wrong about the order of operations. You can't learn to act in the world and learn to understand the world at the same time from a reward signal. You need the understanding first. And that's exactly what changed with large language models — now the prior is there, the model already knows what "checkout" means, and RL becomes the last mile rather than the whole journey. In that sense, World of Bits was a decade early, and a lot of the current agent work is really just that same idea being retried with the missing ingredient finally in place.

r001.rationale: The response says the agent lacked a prior and language understanding, and that large language models later supplied the missing ingredient.

r002.rationale: It discusses hand-built tasks and reward design, but does not identify a lack of people collecting data for labeling as a cause.

astra-6.text:
I think the core problem was that the ambition was ahead of the available learning methods. A general-purpose web agent has to understand what’s on a page, interpret a goal, and carry out a sequence of actions across interfaces it may never have seen before. That’s much harder than learning a policy for one fixed environment.

If you approach that mainly through reinforcement learning, you run into an exploration problem. The agent clicks around, most actions accomplish nothing, and useful feedback may arrive only after a long sequence of correct decisions. When it fails, it’s difficult to learn which step was responsible. And collecting those interactions on the web is slow and messy.

What was missing, in my view, was a strong prior: a model that already understood language, had broad background knowledge, and could make reasonable guesses about how an interface works. Without that foundation, you’re asking reinforcement learning to discover too much from scratch. So I’d interpret the failure as a mismatch between the scope of the goal and the capabilities of the methods at the time, rather than evidence that a general-purpose web agent was fundamentally impossible.

r001.rationale: The response says a strong prior was missing: a model with language understanding and broad background knowledge. This communicates the absence of a foundation model as a reason for the failure.

r002.rationale: The response mentions that web interactions were slow and messy to collect, but does not identify the absence of people collecting data for labeling as a reason for the failure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main issue was that the ambition was ahead of the learning methods available at the time. A web agent has to understand what’s on the screen, figure out what the user wants, and execute a long sequence of actions. With reinforcement learning from scratch, even discovering a successful sequence is difficult. If the agent fails at the end, there’s very little signal telling it which earlier decision was wrong.

And the web isn’t one stable environment. Different websites have different layouts and workflows, so learning to operate one site doesn’t automatically give you a general capability.

I wouldn’t claim to know the internal reasons that particular effort ended. But technically, I think the missing ingredient was a strong starting point: a model that already understands language and has substantial knowledge about the world. That makes learning how to act a much more tractable problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the effort lacked a strong starting model that already understood language and the world, which communicates the absence of a foundation model.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention people collecting data for labeling as a reason for the effort’s failure.
